January 26th, 1943

Dear Willi:

I read the passage of your last letter to Erna, about the relations which we established between R. and authorities here. There are obviously quite a few misunderstandings and misrepresentations, and that's why I use this opportunity to tell you once more in chronological order how things happened and how they were agreed upon.

As you remember, R. used to send his reports through regular mail ever since I arrived here, and we used them as best we could. In the summer of 1941, Paul Vignaux arrived here, of whom you no doubt heard. He was Professor at the Sorbonne, and at the same time one of the leading men in the educational field of the Christian Trade Unions. During the war in France he had been, together with George Lefranc, labor advisor of the French Ministry of Information, and in this capacity we met him quite often.

V. stayed in France until Summer 1941. In the period from the collapse until his departure he had been instrumental in organizing the underground trade union movement, and was particularly helpful in bringing about the close cooperation of the CGT and the Christian Trade Unions. He met R. and Simonne very often, brought him in contact with his friends, and when he arrived here, he immediately got in touch with us. When he saw all the material that we had received from R., he was very much impressed, all the more so as very often these were documents which he himself had either written or seen to it that R. got them. Nobody else here had received any documentation about France at all, regularly and continuously. He told me at that time that he had had ample opportunity to think about R.'s and our group's work, and that he was convinced that only we could make a contribution to the French Labor movement, without which cooperation with America and England was impossible. Ever since that time, we have been closely cooperating with V., who by the way came here with a mandate not only of his own trade unions, but of Jouhaux as well; R. to whom I wrote about it was very pleased about the cooperation which was only the counterpart of his cooperation with V.'s friends over there.

R. kept on asking us to establish another way of communicating with us, so that more confidential information about the labor movement could also get here. When the ILO Conference took place, you remember that Jef and Hauck came here, among others; one of the results was that Jef established a contact to some Washington people for us, about which I wrote you at the time, and about which Jef told you. Still, this was a personal contact only, and nothing very much happened, because at that time the US was not at war, and could or would not do very much to help this special type of work. The real contact took place at the beginning of 1942, through the intermediary of an influential member of the American Labor movement who had become labor advisor of the respective government agency. A conference took place, and it was agreed that the work of R. and the French labor movement which he represented, interested greatly, and that people here were prepared to assist it on lines which I explained to R. in my letter of May 15th, 1942, which was brought to him by messenger, and of which I sent you copy. (Should you not have received that copy, please let me know; I will then send you another one.)

R. and the other friends in France, ours as well as V.'s, were apparently pleased with this arrangement, because from that time on they sent us regularly material, which was very much appreciated here. "Here" means first and above all by our friends and by V., as far as the French movement was concerned. R. was in no way under any obligation towards any authorities, and did not make any reports for them or send to them. The exchange of opinions, however, which we started, did not get us very far, for several reasons, one of which was your request to send all those remarks directly to you. As we could see from casual remarks of R. in different notes, he shared our preoccupations and general opinions.
